title: Deleted calendar events on iPhone: Google and iCloud recovery
description: Check whether an event is missing or deleted, then compare Google Trash with iCloud calendar recovery and their sharing and meeting consequences.
lede: A missing appointment does not always need restoring. First establish where it was stored and whether it still exists there. If it was deleted, the recovery method depends on that provider. This guide is published by Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars.
commonBelief: Restoring a calendar always brings back just the missing appointment, with every invitation and sharing arrangement unchanged.

sections.heading: First separate a missing display from a deleted record
body: Identify the account and calendar that held the appointment, then check its approximate date in the provider’s own calendar. Confirm the signed-in identity, especially when work and personal accounts have similar calendar names. If the event is still there, use the missing-calendar or search guide below. Do not restore data merely because one app cannot display or find it.

A shared calendar that you can no longer access is also a different problem from a deleted event. Ask the owner to confirm the calendar and your access before choosing a recovery operation. For a calendar stored only on a device, do not assume that Google or iCloud holds an independent copy. Avoid adding a second account connection or importing an old file while the original location is uncertain.

sections.heading: For Google, inspect the right calendar’s Trash on a computer
body: Google documents recovery on a computer: open Google Calendar with the relevant account, then Settings > Trash. Each calendar has its own Trash. Restoring requires at least the calendar permission to make changes to events. Identify the intended record before using its Restore control; Google also provides restoration of selected records.

Google normally keeps trashed events for 30 days, but permanent deletion can remove that opportunity. Its spam checks can also place an invitation there. An empty Trash is not proof that you checked the right calendar or have the required access. Consult Google’s current instructions before acting.

sections.heading: Check Google recurrence and meeting consequences
body: Google says instances removed with “This and following events” do not enter Trash and cannot be restored. Other recurring deletions may appear as one grouped row; restoring it can restore multiple deleted instances. Check the scope rather than assuming one row means one date.

When an event creator restores an event, Google says guests must RSVP again. A previously booked room may no longer be available. Compare the restored meeting with its intended participants, dates and resource arrangements before treating it as ready to attend.

sections.heading: For iCloud, understand calendar replacement before proceeding
body: Apple’s iCloud recovery restores an earlier calendar version across devices, replacing the existing calendars. It saves the current version first, but recent changes may be lost. This is not Google’s selected-event Trash workflow. Read Apple’s linked instructions and assess the replacement consequences before choosing an archive.

Apple advises making a backup before restoring. Its documented route is iCloud.com > Data Recovery > Restore Calendars, where available versions are dated. Do not select a version solely because it predates the missing appointment: first consider other changes made since then and what you need to preserve.

sections.heading: Account for iCloud sharing and invitation effects
body: Apple says calendar sharing settings are erased by restoration. You must share your calendars again or ask their owners to share them again. It also describes cases where invitation and cancellation messages are not sent again. Read those details rather than assuming that restoring the calendar reconstructs everyone’s current understanding.

Before deciding, record which calendars you share, who needs access and which arrangements changed recently. Afterward, check access with the people involved and confirm any uncertain meeting directly. Keep this record private; it is a checklist for rebuilding the intended arrangement, not a reason to redistribute invitation links or everyone’s event details.

sections.heading: Use the smallest recovery task that matches the evidence
body: Suppose a club’s Tuesday planning meeting disappears from your phone after you changed next month’s venue. First check the club’s owning account and the Tuesday date. If the meeting remains there, investigate the phone’s view. If it was deleted, establish the provider and the available recovery scope. A dated archive deserves a broader review than a single identified record: the newer venue arrangement also matters.

Write down the intended outcome before acting: recover this appointment, preserve the later venue change and confirm the current participants. Do not turn the exercise into moving the club calendar to another account. After any recovery, compare those specific facts with the organiser rather than assuming that an event with the familiar title means the whole problem is solved.

sections.heading: Verify the result at the source before relying on your phone
body: Recheck the owning calendar, the exact date and time, relevant recurring dates, access and meeting arrangements. Then compare the same event on the iPhone. If the source is correct but the app differs, return to connection, selection and date-coverage checks; do not repeat a recovery operation to force the display to change.

For support, keep a non-sensitive record of the provider, calendar type, approximate date, action taken and where the event is now visible. Omit private links, passwords and confidential notes. These are Google and iCloud procedures, not Cloud Calendars Trash or restore controls. They do not establish recovery options for Outlook, another provider, a device-only calendar or Cloud Calendars sharing data; consult the appropriate service rather than applying these steps to it.

practical: Present at the owning provider, missing on the phone: investigate display, selection, connection and search scope before recovery.
Access to a shared calendar has disappeared: confirm identity and permission with its owner before assuming deletion.
Deleted from a Google calendar: review that calendar’s computer-based Trash and the documented access, recurrence and meeting limits.
Deleted from iCloud: assess the earlier-version replacement and sharing consequences before choosing a recovery version.
Stored somewhere else or location uncertain: identify the actual service and its recovery guidance; do not guess from the app displaying it.
After recovery: compare the original scheduling facts at the provider, confirm uncertain arrangements, then check the phone.

faq.q: The event still appears on the provider’s website. Should I restore a backup?
faq.a: Start with the phone’s account, selected calendar, date range and search behaviour. Preserve the existing provider record; a missing display alone does not establish that data needs restoring.

faq.q: Can I follow these steps for a calendar someone shared with me?
faq.a: First distinguish lost access from deletion and identify who controls the calendar. Use the relevant provider’s permission rules, and involve the owner when needed. Receiving a shared calendar does not by itself establish authority to restore it.

faq.q: Should I import an old ICS file if recovery is unavailable?
faq.a: Treat that as a separate copy/import decision. Check its date, destination and what it preserves using the export guide below. Do not assume that importing recreates the original meeting or its participants’ arrangements.

faq.q: Does Cloud Calendars offer the recovery controls described here?
faq.a: The controls in this guide belong to Google Calendar and iCloud.com. No Cloud Calendars recovery procedure is established here. Identify the event’s storage service before deciding which instructions apply.
